publishedfiledetails.title: Arkham Express
publishedfiledetails.description:
Arkham Express is a free print-and-play cooperative dice-based game designed by David Willems. Players are working together to gather clues, kill monsters, close gates and eventually defeat the Great Old One, Cthulhu.

[h1]Notes[/h1]
The stamina/sanity/investigation counters use states. You can cycle through these states using your number keys or through the right click menu. Alternatively, you can spawn some dice to do the job instead.

publishedfiledetails.title: SPI's Battle of Austerlitz
publishedfiledetails.description: A hex-and-counter wargame from 1980 of the Battle of Austerlitz. Also called the Battle of Three Emperors, it is concidered by some historians to be Napoleon's greatest victory. Designed by David James Ritchie. Moderate complexity, with rulebook & new counter art.

publishedfiledetails.title: Boarding Party
publishedfiledetails.description:
"Boarding Party" is a whimsical strategic resource gathering game in which 4 of the galaxy's top pirates meet aboard a starship to gather party supplies, loot roaming Sentient Vending Machines and harass their opponents to decide who is the Ultimate Party Captain!

Gameplay elements include a unique action programming / tableau hybrid (similar to Mechs Vs Minions), worker placement and management, as well as resource collecting and management.

If you like pina coladas and getting caught in a little bullet rain, this is the game for you!

(constantly uploading edits and new content as it’s finished :)!)

publishedfiledetails.title: Caesar's Legions
publishedfiledetails.description:
Caesar's Legions is a medium complexity wargame simulating the Roman campaigns in Germany at the operational level.

Players choose from 5 scenarios ranging from Caesar's own Germanic campaigns to the Batavian revolt of 70 AD.

Movement is hex based. Tactical cards effect combat resolution which is dice based and cross-referenced on a probability table. Roman units are divided into cohorts. German units are divided into tribes and enjoy hidden movement when in forest terrain.

The game consists of a 22" x 28" map board, over 400 counters (448 counters), playing aids, 16 tactical cards (2 sets of 1 - 8) and a 16-page rulebook.

*Thanks to Mangofeet for Counter Exploder!

publishedfiledetails.title: Co-opoly
publishedfiledetails.description:
In a game jam held in the fall of 2018, we transformed Monopoly into “Co-opoly,” a cooperative board game in which players protest land assemblages and halt the construction of luxury condos. Working together, players bring activists to the city via public transport, then drive these activists (via car co-ops) to locations where they can build tiny homes.

Co-opoly was nominated for an award for "Best Adaptation" by Indiecade 2019.

For more information on Co-opoloy, visit www.monkeymindgames.com.

For more games by Lisa Smedman, visit https://lisasmedman.wixsite.com/author

publishedfiledetails.title: The Business Game - Mine a Million
publishedfiledetails.description:
A game where players open a mine and compete to be the first to reach $1,000,000. The struggle to expand the business, achieve maximum dollar exports and keep ahead of rivals produces one of the most compelling business games ever invented.


The players are operating a mine and trying to get ore to market, but must compete with each other for the limited transportation resources. The ore has to be transported initially by lorries, and then later by barges, to the coastal warehouse. All transport has to be hired and there is always less transport available than required, favouring those who are prepared to take a risk on achieving a quick journey without mishap. For example there are only 5 barges (always one less than the numbers of players) to encourage competition and load sharing. You can also force other players to pay you for taking their ore to make up a barge load as all barges have to travel fully laden. Much depends on how long a journey takes. New ore can only be obtained by throwing a 1 or a six which also triggers the playing of a production card which can be favourable or not.

From the coastal warehouse, barges and ships are used to transport ore out to sea to foreign ports to sell to gradually earn the Million Dollars needed to win the game. The second set of money (dollars) is thus actually a victory point counting device and not actual currency (i.e. it cannot be spent).
It works well with any number of players (when playing with a smaller complement, each player operates multiple mines) except five, as the competition factor on one side of the board is uneven with the other.

publishedfiledetails.title: Fidchell / Gwyddbwyll - the medieval Celtic game of kings
publishedfiledetails.description:
Fidchell (Irish) and Gwyddbwyll (Welsh) was a Celtic boardgame described in the early medieval literature of each culture that was extremely popular before being replaced by the Tafl games during the Viking Age.  While it is described in many sagas, the exact rules were never recorded.  As such, a few different attempts to reconstruct the game have been attempted, but they never seem to feel right for me, they seem to always be off in some way-- particularly I was rather hesitant of a version I've seen with a round board (which doesn't match any known examples of gaming boards from the archaeological record) or versions that show it as a Tafl game (even though the Irish and Welsh Talf variants seem to have been known by different names from Fidchell/Gwyddbwyll).  And so, using the references from the literature, as well as the preserved game from a Romano-British burial in Camulodunum (modern Colchester), I attempted to make my own go at the rules!  I wouldn't go so far as to say I've rediscovered the game as it was, what we do know is still shady enough to be interpretted in different ways, but I think what I have done is made a fun, relatively simple game inspired by the historic fidchell and gwyddbwyll.

The gameboard is gold with silver pieces of the King and his Warriors opposed by Ravens, inspired by the (admittedly, unlikely to be real) descriptions of lavish sets from stories such as Rhonabwy's Dream, Peredur son of Efrawg, and the Wooing of Étaín.  While the look of the game was inspired by the stories, the actual shape and layout was inspired by archaeological examples of Celtic boardgames (particularly the 'doctor's grave' at Camulodunum, mid-1st century AD).  

The rules (which you can find in the Notebook tab in the game, or as the last picture here in the Workshop) were inspired by a mix of the description of play from the medieval stories, some interpretation from the layout of apparently mid-game layouts of the archaeological finds, and finally some comparison with better understood games from the Roman and medieval world.
